Chapter 3: Power, Objectification, and the Making of Sexual Politics
Imagine you’re with a group of friends, talking late into the night—swapping stories about relationships, love, and sex. There’s laughter about awkward moments... and maybe a few secrets come out that have never been shared before. But if you listen closely, there’s something deeper going on. The way we talk about sex isn’t just about what’s happened to us—it’s shaped by something bigger. It’s shaped by power.
In the world of sexual politics, not everyone starts from the same line. For a lot of men, they’re taught early on that their desires matter most. Taking charge is seen as natural—even expected. Women, meanwhile, are often taught to say yes, to be pleasing, to put others first. And it’s not just what families say—these messages are everywhere in the stories and images that surround us.
Pornography is a big part of this landscape. The images you see aren’t just about sex—they’re a lesson in who gets to hold power and who doesn’t. Women are shown as objects, their bodies positioned for someone else’s pleasure. Men are the takers, the conquerors, always in control. Over time, these roles stop feeling like fantasy and start feeling like reality—like this is just the way things are.
Most of us don’t even realize how much this seeps into our own lives. Maybe a woman finds herself saying yes to things she doesn’t really want, just to keep the peace. Or a man feels he has to act tough, hide his feelings, and prove himself through conquest. The rules aren’t written down, but everyone seems to know them.
And here’s something to really notice—these rules don’t just hurt women. They hurt everyone. When sex turns into some kind of contest, where you’re trying to win or avoid losing, the real connection disappears. People start seeing each other as things, not as human beings. The cost? Loneliness, misunderstanding, and that nagging feeling that something important is missing.
Some people do try to break out of these patterns—to build relationships based on respect and equality. But it isn’t easy. The culture keeps pushing back, flooding us with the same old images and stories, making it tough to even imagine something different. It takes real courage to say no, to ask for what you truly want, and to refuse to play by those old rules.
But here’s the good news: change is possible. When you start to notice how power shapes desire—when you say no to treating others as objects—whole new possibilities open up. It’s not easy, and it doesn’t happen overnight. But every single time someone chooses respect over domination, honesty over performance, the world shifts, even if just a little bit.
